strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing visual-token inference costs without retraining. The two-stage design is simple, and its combination of early diversity selection with later visual-token removal is potentially useful.

Results cover eight image and four video benchmarks, with image experiments on both 7B and 13B LLaVA-NeXT. At 10% retention, Table 1 reports 95.1% average relative performance for 7B versus 92.2% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with improvements across all eight image benchmarks.

The evaluation includes measured latency, throughput, and memory rather than relying exclusively on FLOPs. Table 3 reports throughput increasing from 1.5 to 2.8 samples/s and peak memory decreasing from 15.9 to 13.6 GB.

Stage ablations help attribute the gains: diversity selection provides most of the acceleration, while the second stage supplies a smaller additional improvement. Threshold and candidate-layer experiments offer useful sensitivity evidence.
weaknesses: The central attention analysis conflicts with causal masking. Section 3.1 orders tokens as system, visual, then text; Equation (7) explicitly defines attention from query i to key j. Consequently, visual queries cannot attend to subsequent text keys, so alpha_v→t must be zero at every layer. Figure 2 instead shows substantial, varying visual-to-text attention and interprets it as information transfer. This requires correction of the measurement, labeling, or implementation; as written, the claimed bidirectional pruning criterion and its motivation are not technically established.

Originality is insufficiently distinguished from the closest cited work. DivPrune [2] explicitly addresses diversity-based visual-token pruning, while VTW [35] provides information migration and visual-token withdrawal. Neither is evaluated, and the manuscript does not adequately explain the algorithmic distinction from DivPrune. Comparisons against these methods, including a combination of diversity selection and withdrawal, are particularly important because Table 4 attributes most benefits to Stage 1.

Appendix B does not provide a valid theoretical justification. Orthogonal embedding subspaces do not imply statistical independence of arbitrary functions of their coordinates, so Lemma 1 is unsupported. Furthermore, zero covariance does not establish independence. The assumed orthogonal projection scheme is neither part of the implemented method nor verified in the pretrained models. The empirical method may still work, but this proof cannot substantiate the claimed orthogonality or effectiveness of its stages.

Important ablation behavior remains unexplained. In Table 6, checking every deep layer reduces relative performance to 74.3%, versus 98.9% for the default candidate set, while doubling runtime. Additional measurement overhead explains latency but not the accuracy collapse. The paper needs to identify which pruning decisions cause this failure and compare adaptive selection with unconditional removal at matched fixed depths.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. The manuscript does not explain how Equation (7)'s attention probabilities are obtained while preserving efficient-attention execution, or isolate their overhead and greedy-selection cost. Video frame sampling, exact video checkpoint/configuration, generation settings, and positional/KV-cache handling after pruning are insufficiently specified. The 2.6× latency result comes from the four-benchmark ablation, whereas the 95.1% performance figure averages eight benchmarks; these should be presented as distinct measurements. Quantitative long-output speed and quality tests are also absent.

Generality is demonstrated within one model family rather than across architectures. Small Stage 2 improvements lack uncertainty estimates, and several numerical discrepancies weaken reporting precision: the abstract gives a 92.7% runner-up versus Table 1's 92.2%, and the 25% ablation discussion cites timings inconsistent with Table 4. These are correctable issues, but the causal-attention inconsistency and missing closest-method comparisons are substantive reasons for the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision systems problem: reducing visual-token computation without retraining an LVLM. The combination of early diversity-based selection and later visual-token removal is simple and potentially practical.

The reported empirical results are promising across eight image and four video benchmarks. At 10% token retention, Table 1 reports 95.1% average relative performance for LLaVA-NeXT-7B, versus 92.2% for the strongest evaluated baseline. Table 3 reports improved throughput and reduced memory usage.

The manuscript provides algorithm pseudocode, component ablations, threshold and candidate-layer studies, and results for both 7B and 13B models. Table 4 helps establish that most acceleration comes from Stage 1, with a smaller additional benefit from Stage 2.
weaknesses: The central attention criterion is inconsistent with the stated causal decoder. Section 3.1 orders tokens as system, visual, then text; Equation (7) defines attention from visual queries to text keys. Under causal masking, this visual-to-text attention must be zero because the text tokens occur later. Figure 2 nevertheless reports substantial nonzero values and interprets them as information transfer into text. This requires clarification of the actual attention computation, masking, and direction conventions; as written, it undermines both the motivation and reproducibility of Stage 2.

Appendix B does not provide a valid theoretical justification. Orthogonal embedding subspaces do not imply statistical independence of functions of their representations, so Lemma 1's factorization is unsupported. Furthermore, zero covariance does not generally imply independence. The assumed orthogonal projections are neither implemented by ToDRE nor established for the evaluated LVLMs, and the argument supplies no guarantee that pruning preserves task performance.

Originality is insufficiently established against the closest acknowledged work. The manuscript cites DivPrune [2], a diversity-based pruning method, and duplication-focused pruning [54], but does not experimentally compare against them or clearly distinguish their selection mechanisms from its greedy k-center selection. Visual-token withdrawal and information migration are already attributed to VTW [35], which is also absent from the comparisons. These omissions are particularly consequential because Stage 1 accounts for most of the measured benefit, while Stage 2 adds only modest improvements.

The adaptive removal mechanism lacks decisive validation. Table 6 studies candidate layers for threshold checking, but does not compare against unconditional removal at matched fixed layers or report the distribution of selected removal depths. Checking every deep layer reduces performance to 74.3% and approximately doubles runtime; the accompanying discussion explains computational overhead but not the severe accuracy loss. Thus, it remains unclear whether the proposed relevance signal reliably identifies safe removal points.

Efficiency and generalization claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. The headline 2.6× speedup comes from the four-benchmark timing ablation, whereas the directly compared POPE throughput improves by 1.9×. Both can be valid, but their workloads should be distinguished. FlashAttention compatibility is asserted without explaining or benchmarking how the required attention probabilities are obtained. Longer-response advantages receive qualitative examples rather than quantitative latency and quality evaluation, and architecture-agnostic claims are tested only within LLaVA-NeXT.

Important experimental details are missing, including video frame sampling, precise video checkpoint configuration, generation settings, and token-order/position handling after selection. Baselines are excluded from some settings because of reported transfer failures without numerical results or sufficient adaptation details. Reporting also needs correction: the abstract/contributions cite a 92.7% runner-up rather than Table 1's 92.2%, and the 25% ablation timing in the prose disagrees with Table 4. These reporting errors are secondary to the substantive methodological and comparison concerns above.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing LVLM inference cost without retraining. Combining early diversity-based selection with later visual-token removal is simple and potentially useful.

The reported accuracy–efficiency trade-off is promising. At 10% token retention, Table 1 reports 95.1% average relative performance for LLaVA-NeXT-7B, versus 92.2% for GlobalCom2. Table 3 reports throughput increasing from 1.5 to 2.8 samples/s and peak memory decreasing from 15.9 to 13.6 GB.
Evaluation covers eight image and four video benchmarks, two model sizes, and two compression ratios. Table 2 suggests that substantial compression can preserve video understanding performance.

The component ablation in Table 4 usefully separates the stages: diversity-based selection provides most of the acceleration, while subsequent removal offers a modest additional benefit. Threshold and candidate-layer ablations provide further empirical context.
weaknesses: The central attention criterion is inconsistent with causal attention as defined. Section 3.1 orders tokens as system, visual, then text; Equation (7) defines attention from visual queries to subsequent text keys. Under the decoder's causal mask, this visual-to-text quantity must be zero at every layer. Figure 2 nevertheless shows substantial nonzero values and interprets them as visual information entering text tokens, reversing the stated query/key direction. The authors need to reconcile the equation, masking, plotted measurements, and implementation. This directly affects the scientific justification and reproducibility of Stage 2.

Appendix B does not establish the claimed theoretical result. Geometric orthogonality alone does not imply the statistical independence asserted in Lemma 1, and zero covariance does not generally establish independence. Moreover, the orthogonal modality subspaces are neither enforced by ToDRE nor demonstrated in the evaluated models. The argument therefore cannot validate the two-stage method as claimed.

Originality and comparative evidence are insufficiently established against the closest cited work. DivPrune [2] explicitly concerns diversity-based token pruning, and VTW [35] already motivates visual-token withdrawal through information migration, yet neither is experimentally compared. The manuscript should distinguish its selection rule from DivPrune and compare its adaptive withdrawal against VTW and fixed-layer withdrawal at matched computational budgets. Comparisons mainly against attention-based methods do not isolate the proposed advance.

Table 6 contains an unexplained result that raises implementation concerns: checking every deep layer produces 74.3% relative performance and takes 155:01, compared with 98.9% and 72:46 for the selected checkpoints. Additional measurement overhead can explain runtime, but not the large accuracy collapse. The paper needs to explain which pruning decisions change and why; the current discussion attributes the problem primarily to overhead.

Important implementation and evaluation details are missing. The manuscript does not explain how the attention ratios are obtained while preserving the claimed efficient-attention compatibility, or clearly specify video frame sampling, exact video checkpoint configuration, decoding settings, and treatment of token positions after pruning. It also lacks a breakdown of selection and attention-measurement overhead. These omissions limit reproducibility and assessment of the architecture-agnostic claim, which is tested only within the LLaVA-NeXT family.

The evidence for the distinctive second stage remains limited. Table 4 shows only small incremental accuracy and runtime gains over Stage 1, without uncertainty estimates or a comparison against simpler withdrawal rules. Claimed advantages for long generation are supported by qualitative examples rather than quantitative latency and quality measurements. Overall, the empirical promise is substantial, but the unresolved attention inconsistency, invalid theoretical argument, and missing closest-baseline comparisons favor rejection under the Algorithms/General criteria.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing LVLM inference costs without retraining. The two-stage design is straightforward, and the supplementary pseudocode makes the diversity-selection procedure understandable.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering twelve image/video benchmarks and four model configurations. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, Table 1 reports 95.0% normalized performance at 10% token retention, compared with 93.5% for DivPrune. Table 4 reports substantial reductions in FLOPs and memory, with throughput increasing from 1.5 to 2.9 samples/s.

The component ablations support a useful practical contribution from both stages. In Table 5, adding Stage 2 reduces runtime from 31:18 to 29:43 at 10% retention with essentially unchanged accuracy. Additional pivot, threshold, and layer-selection experiments help characterize the design.
weaknesses: The central attention analysis conflicts with the stated causal decoder setup. Section 3.1 orders tokens as system, visual, then text. Under causal attention, visual queries cannot attend to subsequent text keys, so the visual-to-text ratio in Eq. (8) should be identically zero. Figure 2 nevertheless reports substantial visual-to-text attention. The paper needs to explain the actual token ordering, masking, and measurement procedure; otherwise, the bidirectional information-migration interpretation and one half of the pruning criterion are unsupported.

The claimed proof of orthogonality is mathematically unjustified. Supplementary Lemma 1 treats orthogonal embedding subspaces as sufficient for statistical independence, which does not hold generally. The subsequent conclusion also conflates zero covariance with independence. Furthermore, the orthogonal projections assumed by the analysis are neither implemented nor established for the evaluated pretrained models. This undermines an explicitly advertised contribution, although it does not by itself invalidate the empirical heuristic.

The incremental contribution relative to the closest methods is insufficiently isolated. Diversity-based selection is already represented by DivPrune, and information migration and visual-token withdrawal are explicitly attributed to VTW. There is no direct VTW comparison, no DivPrune-plus-Stage-2 baseline, and no matched comparison against unconditional removal at the same 7L/8 layer. These controls are important for establishing the value of max-sum selection and the proposed task-relevance gate.

The evidence for adaptive, task-dependent removal is limited. The implementation checks a single prescribed depth, but does not report how frequently removal is triggered, how this varies across questions or backbones, or whether attention predicts pruning-induced errors. Small attention mass alone does not establish that visual information has been safely transferred. The supplementary layer ablation shows substantial degradation from earlier removal, emphasizing the need to validate this decision rule.

Efficiency and reproducibility details are incomplete. The manuscript claims compatibility with efficient attention operators while requiring attention probabilities, but does not explain how those statistics are obtained or account separately for their overhead and the sequential greedy selection. Video frame sampling, inference precision, batching, generation settings, retained-token positional handling, and KV-cache handling need specification. The 2.6× aggregate runtime result and 1.9× POPE throughput result concern different measurements and should be clearly distinguished.

Several experimental claims need tighter support. Table 3 tests additional backbones without competing pruning methods, so it demonstrates applicability rather than comparative superiority. The video advantage over DivPrune is only 0.2–0.6 normalized percentage points, without uncertainty estimates. Table 1 and Table 5 also disagree on the same 10%-retention ToDRE configuration for MME and ScienceQA. These discrepancies require explanation, while the anticipated benefits for long generation remain supported only by qualitative examples.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing LVLM inference cost without retraining. The combination of early diversity-based token selection and late visual-token removal is simple and potentially useful.

The reported empirical coverage is substantial: twelve image/video benchmarks and four model configurations. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, Table 1 reports 95.0% normalized average performance at 10% token retention, versus 93.5% for DivPrune. Table 4 reports reduced memory and improved throughput relative to the uncompressed model.

The component ablations provide useful evidence beyond aggregate benchmark scores. Table 5 shows that Stage 2 reduces runtime from 31:18 to 29:43 after aggressive Stage 1 pruning with little accuracy change. Supplementary experiments examine pivot selection, thresholds, and pruning depth.
weaknesses: The claimed proof of orthogonality is mathematically unsound. Supplementary Lemma 1 assumes that orthogonal embedding subspaces imply statistical independence of arbitrary similarity and relevance functions; geometric orthogonality does not establish that factorization. The subsequent covariance calculation simply relies on this unsupported lemma, and zero covariance would not generally imply independence either. Moreover, the orthogonal embedding scheme assumed in the analysis is neither implemented nor demonstrated in the evaluated pretrained models. This undermines an explicitly advertised contribution, although it does not by itself invalidate the empirical results.

The Stage 2 attention criterion conflicts with the stated causal token ordering. Section 3.1 places system tokens before visual tokens and question tokens after them. Under causal masking, visual queries cannot attend to subsequent question keys, so the visual-to-text numerator in Eq. (8) should be zero at every layer. Figure 2 nevertheless reports substantial nonzero visual-to-text attention. The paper must clarify the actual masks, token groups, and measurement procedure; as written, the claimed bidirectional information-migration evidence is inconsistent with the model description.

The experiments do not isolate the main algorithmic advances sufficiently. Diversity-based pruning already appears in DivPrune, and information migration and complete visual-token removal are explicitly attributed to VTW. However, VTW is absent from the quantitative comparisons, and there is no controlled comparison of max-sum versus DivPrune's selection objective with identical pivots and Stage 2, or adaptive removal versus unconditional removal at the same late layer. Table 5 establishes a benefit from adding late pruning, but does not establish that the proposed relevance criterion is responsible.

Reproducibility of the efficiency and compatibility claims is incomplete. The manuscript does not adequately specify video frame sampling, generation settings, timing batch size and precision, positional-index handling after pruning, or which layers retain visual KV-cache entries. It also claims full compatibility with efficient attention operators while requiring attention-probability sums, without explaining their implementation and overhead. These details are consequential for reproducing the runtime gains and understanding the benefits during long generation.

Some empirical claims exceed the evidence. Qwen and InternVL results compare only against their uncompressed models, so they establish applicability rather than superiority over competing pruning methods on those architectures. The video advantage over DivPrune is only 0.2 percentage points in normalized average performance at 10% retention, without uncertainty estimates. Greater benefits for long outputs are supported by qualitative examples rather than quantitative latency-versus-output-length measurements.

Several reporting discrepancies need reconciliation. At 10% retention, Table 1 gives ToDRE MME/ScienceQA scores of 1464.4/70.2, whereas Table 5 gives 1469.3/70.5 for the apparently same configuration. The headline 2.6× speedup and 95.0% performance also combine the four-benchmark timing study with the eight-benchmark accuracy average; the directly reported POPE throughput speedup is 1.9×. These results can coexist, but the scope of the headline claim should be explicit.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing LVLM inference costs without retraining. The two-stage approach is straightforward, and the diversity-selection algorithm is clearly specified with supplementary pseudocode.

The empirical coverage is substantial: twelve image/video benchmarks, four model configurations, and two retention ratios. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, Table 1 reports 95.0% normalized performance at 10% retention, versus 93.5% for DivPrune, with improvements across all eight image benchmarks.

The efficiency measurements demonstrate useful practical savings. Table 4 reports throughput increasing from 1.5 to 2.9 samples/s and peak memory decreasing from 15.9 to 13.6 GB. Table 5 separately supports approximately 2.6× acceleration for its aggregate timing workload.

Component, pivot-selection, threshold, and layer ablations help characterize the method. Table 5 shows that the second stage provides additional time savings beyond diversity selection while approximately preserving accuracy.
weaknesses: The attention-based justification has a consequential inconsistency. Section 3.1 orders tokens as system, visual, then text. Under causal attention, visual queries cannot attend to subsequent text keys, so the visual-to-text ratio defined in Eq. (8) should be zero. Figure 2 nevertheless reports substantial nonzero visual-to-text attention. The paper must explain the actual masking, token grouping, and measurement procedure; otherwise one half of the proposed bidirectional criterion is vacuous and the central information-migration evidence is questionable.

The claimed orthogonality proof is invalid. Supplementary Lemma 1 infers statistical independence from orthogonal embedding subspaces, which does not follow without additional distributional assumptions. The concluding inference from zero covariance to independence is also invalid in general. Moreover, the assumed orthogonal embedding construction is neither implemented nor established for the evaluated pretrained models. This undermines an explicitly advertised contribution, although it does not by itself invalidate the empirical algorithm.

The distinctive value of adaptive task-relevance pruning is insufficiently isolated. Section 4.2 evaluates the criterion only at 7L/8, making the default procedure effectively a conditional removal at a fixed depth. There is no matched comparison against unconditional removal at that depth, no report of how often the condition triggers, and no direct experimental comparison with VTW despite its close relationship. Comparing max-sum and DivPrune-style selection under identical pivots and second-stage pruning would also better establish the source of improvement.

Efficiency reproducibility needs more detail. The manuscript does not adequately specify batch size, numerical precision, attention backend, video frame sampling, or the workload underlying aggregate timings. The claimed compatibility with efficient attention operators needs an implementation explanation because Eq. (8) requires attention probabilities that standard FlashAttention interfaces do not expose. Long-generation efficiency benefits remain an expectation rather than a quantitatively demonstrated result.

Some experimental claims exceed the evidence. Qwen and InternVL evaluations lack competing pruning baselines, so they establish applicability rather than comparative superiority across architectures. The 0.2-point normalized advantage over DivPrune on video at 10% retention is small and lacks uncertainty estimates. Additionally, the same apparent 10% ToDRE configuration gives different MME/ScienceQA results in Tables 1 and 5, requiring clarification. Overall, the promising practical results do not yet outweigh the unresolved methodological and evidential concerns under an Algorithms/General assessment.
